11881-the-shadow-of-the-north-a-story-of:
Joseph A. Altsheler's 1917 novel belongs to his French and Indian War series, following Robert Lennox, a lad of unknown origin, Tayoga, a young Onondaga warrior, and the hunter David Willet. A long cast list sets them among French officers, British generals, and Mohawk leaders such as Joseph Brant.

The story moves between old New York and wilderness campaigns, with blockhouses, pack horses, and rifle work in the forest. Altsheler treats the lost campaign of the title as a test of loyalty and endurance, where young soldiers learn war not from parade grounds but from cold, distance, and sudden attack.
1217-penelope-s-experiences-in-scotland-:
Kate Douglas Wiggin sends Penelope, her American traveler, to Scotland, where she tours castles, lochs, and villages and writes home in letters full of humor and affection. The tale follows Penelope and her friends through Edinburgh, the Highlands, and country inns, meeting lairds, guides, and ghosts.

Wiggin writes Scotland with a tourist's delight and a novelist's eye for character. The book is light, sunny, and full of local color. It suits readers who like gentle travel tales and the Scotland of storybooks. Wiggin's Scotland letters still charm travelers and armchair tourists alike.
12518-the-adventures-of-a-forty-niner-an:
Daniel Knower's 1894 account describes California and San Francisco in the gold-rush years, through events and ideas of those early days. Knower dedicates the book to Stevenson, Frémont and Sutter, three pre-eminent pioneers of California, and recalls a society formed to preserve the memory of that time.

Membership in that society required arrival in California before 1 January 1850, a rule that marks the forty-niner generation. Knower writes of camps, streets, people and customs, mixing personal memory with history. The book serves as a vivid, partisan record of a city built in haste, told by a man who was there.
131-the-pilgrim-s-progress-from-this-wor:
Christian flees the City of Destruction with a burden on his back and a book in his hand. John Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, told as a dream, follows him toward the Celestial City. The Slough of Despond, Vanity Fair, and the Giant Despair block his road.

Faithful, Hopeful, and Evangelist help or warn him, while flatterers and tyrants mislead him. Bunyan's allegory turns doctrine into inns, hills, and battles a reader can picture. Part One stands complete on its own. The book became, after the Bible, the most read work in English.
1358-enoch-arden-c:
Alfred Tennyson's poem tells of Enoch Arden, a fisherman who sails and is wrecked, spending years marooned on a desert island while his wife Annie, believing him dead, marries his friend Philip. Enoch returns at last, sees his wife happy, and chooses silence over ruin.

Tennyson writes the tale in blank verse of grave beauty, and Enoch's self-denial gives it its pathos. The poem was a bestseller in its day and inspired plays and films. It remains a moving study of love, loss, and noble restraint. Tennyson's verse gives Enoch's self-denial its full pathos.
13589-the-theory-of-the-theatre-and-othe:
Clayton Hamilton's Theory of the Theatre and Other Principles of Dramatic Criticism, uniform with his Studies in Stagecraft, examines how plays work on stage. The companion volume covers the new art of making plays, the pictorial stage, the decorative drama, and the drama of illusion. It also covers stage direction and a plea for a new type of play.

Hamilton describes an Elizabethan stage with an arras drawn aside to reveal a bed or banqueting board. An upper room serves for Juliet's balcony or a commandant on city walls, and properties move on and off like the trellised arbor in The Spanish Tragedy. A dramatist, he warns, is at actors' mercy: a delicate love scene can be spoiled by an actor without feeling, or a cruel character softened by too charming a player.
17374-bank-of-the-manhattan-company-char:
The Bank of the Manhattan Company, of 40 Wall Street, New York, issued this account of its origin, history, and progress, as a progressive commercial bank chartered in 1799. The story opens on May 8, 1799, when the committee on by-laws reported a common seal for the corporation, showing Oceanus, a god of the sea, seated in state. That old seal marks a bank born with the young republic.

Readers follow the bank from its charter through growth into a major New York institution, with attention to its business and its place in the city. The volume serves local historians, banking historians, and anyone curious about how an early American bank presented its own past. Its tone is proud, as befits a corporate history.
17546-the-lion-of-saint-mark-a-story-of-:
G. A. Henty set this adventure story in Venice in the fourteenth century, under the sign of the Lion of Saint Mark. Chapters open with Venice itself and a conspiracy, then move to the Grand Canal, a carrying off, a clue, and a hut on San Nicolo. A trader's ship, an attack by pirates, the capture of the Lido, and a recapture follow, with battles at Antium and Pola ahead.

Young readers follow a hero through Venetian politics, sea fights, and escapes, in Henty's brisk, instructive style. The book mixes history with adventure, teaching something of Venice's power while keeping the pace quick. It remains a sturdy example of Henty's historical tales for boys.
17973-the-world-of-romance-being-contrib:
William Morris wrote The World of Romance, gathering his tales from the Oxford and Cambridge Magazine of 1856, printed in London in 1906 by J. Thomson. Morris, still a student, had paid for the magazine himself, with Rossetti among its writers, and it ran just twelve issues.

The tales live in pure romance: medieval customs, buildings, faith, and the social frame of the 1200s and 1300s, set in no known age or land. The Story of the Unknown Church opens the set, told by a mason whose church vanished two centuries past. Morris later called these tales crude and young, yet they glow with his early fire.
18696-the-olden-time-series-vol-6-litera:
Henry M. Brooks compiled this sixth volume of Ye Olden Time Series at Boston in 1886 with Ticknor and Company. The series gleans items from old newspapers, chiefly of Boston and Salem, with brief comments by Brooks. Earlier volumes covered lotteries, spinning wheels, Sundays, advertisements, and punishments; this one turns to literary curiosities.

An index of names runs from John Adams and Anne Bradstreet to Benedict Arnold and Major Andre, showing the range of scraps within. Brooks offers amusement for young and old plus raw stuff for students of New England history. The book is a charming dip into old print culture.
19422-the-organization-of-the-congregati:
Beale M. Schmucker wrote this study of how early Lutheran congregations in America formed and governed themselves, first printed in a church review in the late eighteen hundreds. Free from state control for the first time, these groups had to settle their own rules for pastors, members, and church order.

The study draws on early constitutions, including that of Augustus Church, and on the work of Henry Muhlenberg in shaping common practice. It shows how a shared confession, above all the Augsburg Confession, gave scattered immigrant churches a common frame without a state church to hold them.
19765-vikings-of-the-pacific-the-adventu:
A. C. Laut's Vikings of the Pacific, from 1905, tells of explorers who came to America's West Coast. Laut opens with a credo: man can become master of his destiny. We forget, she writes, that people can fight and remake their own surroundings. Her explorers are exhibits for that claim. They are the sea rovers and fur traders of the North Pacific.

Laut wrote popular history with a novelist's pace. Russian, Spanish, British, and American adventurers crowd these coasts. Their story runs from Bering's voyages toward settled trade. She treats them as Vikings for their daring, not their blood. The book is romantic history, proud and brisk. It preserves an early Canadian voice on the Pacific past.
19768-professor-royce-s-libel-a-public-a:
Professor Royce's Libel is a public appeal for redress addressed to Harvard University. Its author felt attacked in print and little defended. He writes that speaking out would seem needless if Harvard itself were not involved. An attack otherwise unworthy of notice drew his answer for that reason. The pamphlet is self-defense conducted before the public. Academic honor in that era was fought in pamphlets.

Such appeals were the op-eds of the nineteenth century. A scholar's name was his capital, and libel threatened it directly. The author asks the university community to judge his case. Readers meet the raw etiquette of old academic feuds. The heat is real, even when the cause is forgotten.
20136-the-seventeenth-highland-light-inf:
The Seventeenth Highland Light Infantry, Glasgow Chamber of Commerce Battalion, kept a war history. Its field narrative stays close to the battalion's own share of the campaign. The history committee barred any wide view of the whole war. Other units and grand strategy sit outside its chosen scope.

Glasgow raised this battalion from its chamber of commerce circles. Clerks and business men served in its ranks on the western front. Unit histories like this one list actions, losses, and names with care. They let families trace where their men fought, fell, and endured.
20322-notes-and-queries-number-188-june-:
Notes and Queries, number 188, for June 4, 1853, is a journal of shared learning. Its subtitle calls it a medium of inter-communication for literary men. Readers wrote in with questions, answers, and small finds on books and history. One note quotes a writer who vows to fix two faulted lines.

He will let his enemy do him a kindness where harm was meant. Such exchanges built a vast store of notes on words, graves, and customs. Scholars and keen amateurs still mine old Notes and Queries volumes. This number gives a neat taste of Victorian learning by post.
20361-the-voice-of-the-machines-an-intro:
The Voice of the Machines introduces the twentieth century through its machines. The machine, it argues, is a wholly new fact in human life. In importance and in shaping daily life, it has no precedent. The machine has no traditions of its own to draw on.

To take a traditional stand on life, one must leave the machine out. It has always been left out, the writer notes with irony. Yet leaving it out now changes little, as machines rule more. Readers get an early, sharp essay on technology's rise and its cost.
20408-notes-and-queries-number-185-may-1:
Dated May 14, 1853, number 185 of Notes and Queries carries the usual mix of queries, replies, and short learned notes. Its readers chased exact facts about books, authors, inscriptions, and customs. No topic was too small if it could be settled by proof.

One note marvels at the fate of the Emblems of Alciatus. The book passed through countless editions and was translated into most languages of the continent. Yet no version was ever printed in England, though English readers knew the work. The item shows the journal at work on the odd gaps in book history.
20409-notes-and-queries-number-186-may-2:
Number 186 of Notes and Queries came out on May 21, 1853. Like every issue, it prints brief notes and answers sent in by readers. Church history, old authors, and points of language all find a place in its columns.

One note corrects every edition of a work that prints the name Osorius. The name, the writer argues, must be a mere misprint. The man was no Portuguese bishop but a Spaniard, born at Tarragona. Other notes follow Saint Augustine on a mission to Jerusalem. The issue shows Victorian scholars mending small errors with great care.
20410-notes-and-queries-number-187-may-2:
Number 187 of Notes and Queries is dated May 28, 1853. The journal served as a shared notebook for readers who studied old books and records. Its pages carry queries, replies, and corrections from across the country.

One note takes up the memoir printed with the 1845 Aldine edition of Chaucer's poems. There Sir Harris Nicolas argues that Chaucer did not know the Italian language. If true, the poet could not have drawn directly on Italian books. The note shows how the journal's readers tested big claims about famous authors against hard evidence. Small facts, firmly settled, were the journal's pride.
21894-the-rover-boys-at-colby-hall-or-th:
A second generation of Rovers goes to school in The Rover Boys at Colby Hall, by Arthur M. Winfield, the pen name of Edward Stratemeyer. Tom Rover's twins are chips of the old block, Sam Rover says, with a capital I. The frontispiece shows Jack Rover starting down the football field with the ball. Colby Hall is a military school, and its young cadets struggle through studies, sports, and scrapes.

Stratemeyer built the Rover Boys into one of the best-loved boys' series in America. This volume opens the second series, handing the flag to the sons of the first heroes. The formula is intact: clean fun, loyal friends, and bullies beaten fairly. Generations of boys learned series reading on books like this one.
22117-across-coveted-lands-or-a-journey-:
A. Henry Savage Landor crossed Asia in the journey told in Across Coveted Lands. His route ran overland from Flushing in Holland all the way to Calcutta. He left his baggage registered for Warsaw, crossed by night boat, and sped by express through Berlin. Ahead lay Russia, Persia, and Baluchistan, lands coveted by rival empires.

Landor describes courts, deserts, caravans, and the politics of the Great Game. Britain and Russia watched every road he travelled. His drawings and photographs filled the published volumes. Landor was a showman as well as a traveller, and his books sold adventure with real geography. This one covers the classic overland route to India.
22126-notes-and-queries-number-35-june-2:
Notes and Queries was a weekly paper where scholars answered each other's questions by post. Number 35, dated June 29, 1850, shows the young journal at work. Its motto, borrowed from Captain Cuttle, is "When found, make a note of." Antiquaries, genealogists, and literary men crowd its columns.

One note untangles two Gorings, father and son, both Earls of Norwich in the Civil War years. Careless compilers had merged the men; a careful reader separates them. Around such notes sit queries on proverbs, books, inscriptions, and family arms. The journal trained Victorian scholarship to work in public. Single issues like this one are bricks in that great shared notebook.
22127-notes-and-queries-number-34-june-2:
Number 34 of Notes and Queries appeared on June 22, 1850, in the journal's first year. The weekly paper linked literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists across Britain. Readers sent questions; other readers answered them in print. Its notes open with Henry Nicholas, founder of the Family of Love.

Nicholas, a Westphalian who lived at Amsterdam and Emden, styled himself a deified man. The note traces his sect's strange career from about 1540. Other columns handle ballads, epitaphs, and points of local history. Reading one issue shows the machine working: small facts, carefully checked, passed hand to hand. Notes and Queries ran for more than a century on that simple plan.
22793-the-standard-oratorios-their-stori:
George P. Upton wrote The Standard Oratorios: Their Stories, Their Music, and Their Composers, a handbook for concert-goers in the great age of choral societies. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. When every city had its Handel festival, listeners needed a guide to the works, their plots, and their makers.

The preface promises that each oratorio is described as fully as its brief allotment of space allows. The author says the utmost pains went into historical and chronological accuracy. Such details, he notes, are nearly always matters of controversy. Handel, Haydn, and Mendelssohn anchor the canon the book surveys. Upton wrote a shelf of such standard guides, and this one taught Victorian and American audiences how to hear their favorite sacred dramas.
23204-notes-and-queries-number-70-march-:
Number 70 of Notes and Queries, dated March 1, 1851, is one issue of a weekly journal where readers traded notes, questions, and answers on books, history, and old customs. One item in this issue makes a grand appeal. Its writer calls on the literary men of England, the government, and the public to back a glorious expedition.

He urges them to keep in mind words set at the head of his article, drawn from a much-loved author. The mix is typical of the journal: bold public proposals sit beside small points of learning. Readers get a lively record of Victorian curiosity at work.
23205-notes-and-queries-number-71-march-:
Number 71 of Notes and Queries, dated March 8, 1851, continues the weekly exchange of literary notes and questions. One note turns to Shakespeare. Its writer picks out a few passages in All's Well That Ends Well that, he says, have had little light thrown on them despite all that has been written.

The passage in question shows Bertram pressing Diana to give in to his wishes. Notes like this were the journal's trade: a reader flags a hard line, and other readers answer in later issues. The result is a slow, public seminar on classic texts, run in print.
23402-notes-and-queries-number-75-april-:
Notes and Queries, a weekly medium for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, filled this number of early April, eighteen fifty one, with notes, queries, and replies. Its motto bids the reader, when found, make a note of it, and the pages live up to that call.

Inside, Edward Foss writes on two chancellors, Bolton Corney on a Carolina lament, and folk lore notes cover cures for whooping cough, Devon charms, and Lent lilies. Queries chase poems of John Seguard of Norwich, an epitaph for the Countess of Pembroke, the sense of a word, and the arms of Robert Nelson. For lovers of old books and odd facts, the issue is a lively window onto Victorian learned talk.
23956-anti-slavery-opinions-before-the-y:
William Frederick Poole, librarian of the Public Library of Cincinnati, read Anti-Slavery Opinions Before the Year 1800 before the Cincinnati Literary Club on November 16, 1872. Robert Clarke and Company published it in 1873, with a facsimile reprint of an even rarer document appended.

Poole examines anti-slavery opinion in America just before 1800, using a rare pamphlet from George Washington's library, then kept at the Boston Athenaeum, which had bought the collection in 1849. The appendix reprints Dr. George Buchanan's oration on the moral and political evil of slavery, delivered at Baltimore on July 4, 1791, before the Maryland Society for Promoting the Abolition of Slavery.
25683-the-escape-of-a-princess-pat-being:
George Pearson tells the escape of a Princess Pat soldier in this full account. Corporal Edwards served in Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry. He was captured and held fifteen months. He then escaped from Germany into Holland. Corporal, now Sergeant, Edward Edwards fronts the book in a portrait.

Chapters open at Polygon Wood, Ypres, and Hill 60, preparing for gas, then the fourth of May and an unofficial armistice. Corporal Edwards takes up the tale among the wounded, and Major Gault comes back with news of a king dead and a king living. Capture, prison, and a final dash to Holland close a First World War memoir.
25894-the-spirit-proper-to-the-times-a-s:
James Walker preached this sermon at King's Chapel, Boston, on Sunday, May 12, 1861, at the start of the Civil War. Taking for his text the verse that God is well pleased with such sacrifices, Walker speaks of public spirit as a willingness to give up goods for the public good. Since no one can have everything, he says, we must yield some things to gain or secure others.

Walker notes that wicked men and worldly men both live by sacrifice, the one giving health and name to vice, the miser giving all that makes life worth having to his hoard. The country at war asks sacrifices of property, labor, and life, and Walker finds men ready to give, not grudgingly or of necessity. Printed at the wardens' request, the sermon calls a prosperous nation to bear war's cost with open hands.
27538-notes-and-queries-no-209-october-2:
Notes and Queries, a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, published this number, 209, on Saturday, 29 October 1853, at fourpence. Its motto comes from Captain Cuttle: when found, make a note of.

Notes in this number treat the Scottish national records, Patrick Carey, an inedited lyric by Felicia Hemans, and Shakespeare correspondence. Minor notes cover monumental inscriptions, Marlborough at Blenheim, and the etymology of till and until. Queries ask about polarised light and dramatic representations. The issue shows Victorian scholarship in weekly conversation with itself. Green Eyes, by Harry Leroy Temple, gets a note too.
27583-the-importance-of-the-proof-reader:
John Wilson, formerly proprietor of the University Press, read this paper on the importance of the proof-reader before the Club of Odd Volumes in Boston. The University Press published it in Cambridge in 1901, and reprinted it in 1922 after Wilson's death in 1903.

Wilson names author, compositor, and proof-reader as the three makers of a book in press. The true proof-reader, he argues, should be a practical printer and also a lover of literature, at home in the classics of every tongue and in science's results. His paper draws on fifty years in the printing trade, and defends a craft readers seldom notice.
27629-captain-desmond-v-c:
Maud Diver, author of The Great Amulet and Candles in the Wind, published this revised edition of Captain Desmond, V.C., in large part rewritten, with William Blackwood and Sons in Edinburgh and London in 1917. She dedicates it to her son Cyril and to Mrs. Alan Batten, for generous help and interest.

Diver's epigraph, from Robert Browning, praises a man who never retreats, but marches breast forward, and never doubts the clouds will break. In revising, she brought the aftermath nearer her original conception, replacing one final scene with three short chapters. She had suppressed them at first for fear of making the book too long, and risked upsetting the balance of sympathy.
27679-uncle-sam-s-boys-as-sergeants-or-h:
H. Irving Hancock, author of Uncle Sam's Boys in the Ranks and Uncle Sam's Boys in the Philippines, published this boys' army story with Henry Altemus of Philadelphia in 1911, illustrated. Its heroes handle their first real commands as sergeants.

Chapters open with a tip-off by wig-wag, Lieutenant Algy joining the army, and the first breath against a soldier's honor. Corporal Hal's admission, the squad room turning cold, and the racking of the new sergeant follow. Sergeant Overton and discipline, Hal riding into treachery, and chasing a speeding deserter come later. A frontispiece shows Private Hinkey howling: Hey, you idiot.
28474-notes-and-queries-number-192-july-:
Saturday, July 2, 1853, brought number 192 of Notes and Queries, a weekly medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, priced at fourpence. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, reads: When found, make a note of it.

Notes in this number include the oblation of a white bull, Newstead Abbey, and celebrated passages in Romeo and Juliet and King Lear. Queries ask whether Captain Cook first discovered the Sandwich Islands and about superstitions of Cornish miners. Replies, photographic correspondence, and notices to correspondents fill out a lively record of Victorian scholarly curiosity in miniature.
28475-notes-and-queries-number-193-july-:
July 9, 1853, saw number 193 of Notes and Queries, the weekly journal for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, priced at fourpence. Its notes open with the eye and its primary idea, followed by gossiping history, De Quincey's account of Hatfield, and the names of early inhabitants of Hellas.

Shakespeare Readings number nine and Goethe's author-remuneration follow, with minor notes on parallel passages, unpublished epitaphs, and Napoleon's bees. The main query asks whether Thomas Lord Lyttelton wrote Junius's letters. Replies on wild plants, heraldry, and serpents, with photographic correspondence on the camera obscura, complete the number.
29412-the-phantom-world-or-the-philosoph:
Augustine Calmet's Phantom World, translated from the French with a preface and notes by the Rev. Henry Christmas, surveys the history and philosophy of spirits and apparitions. The Philadelphia edition of 1850, two volumes in one, opens with good angels proved from the Old and New Testaments, then moves through apparitions, hauntings, and the claims of the unseen. Christmas, librarian of Sion College, frames Calmet's learning with English notes.

Calmet argues with care: many tales of spirits rest on error, yet behind most human errors lies some grain of truth. The book weighs scripture, history, and reason side by side. Students of folklore, demonology, and the history of belief will find a learned, sober classic on why ghosts have haunted human thought for so long.
30914-the-corner-house-girls-growing-up-:
Grace Brooks Hill wrote this 1918 book in the Corner House Girls series, published by Barse and Hopkins in Newark and New York, with pictures by R. Emmett Owen. Earlier books in the series include The Corner House Girls, The Corner House Girls at School, Under Canvas, In a Play, Odd Find, and On a Tour. The frontispiece shows Ruth springing forward and seizing an old gentleman's coat.

Chapters run from All Up in the Air and The Old Gentleman with the Green Umbrella. They pass through The Aerial Tramway, School in the Offing, The Shepards, Naming the New Baby, and A Feline Furor. They continue with Neighbor, Everything at Sixes and at Sevens, Aboard the Nancy Hanks, and Afloat on the Canal. They end with Missing and The Hue and Cry. It is a sequel in a long-running girls' series, following the Corner House girls as they grow up.
31378-notes-and-queries-number-237-may-1:
Dated Saturday, May 13, 1854, issue number 237 of Notes and Queries presents itself as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, credited to Captain Cuttle, runs "When found, make a note of." Contents include a note on Shakespeare's rime made at the Mytre by Dr. E. F. Rimbault, a piece on Rous, the Scottish psalmist and provost of Eton, and original English royal letters to the grand masters of Malta by William Winthrop.

Notes, minor queries, and replies fill the rest of the issue, with readers asking and answering questions on history, language, and antiquities. The weekly format made it a clearinghouse for small facts that larger books overlooked. For modern researchers, the issue is a compact record of what Victorian antiquaries were curious about, week by week.
31398-notes-and-queries-number-238-may-2:
Dated Saturday, May 20, 1854, issue number 238 of Notes and Queries presents itself as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, credited to Captain Cuttle, runs "When found, make a note of." Short notes, minor queries, and replies fill its pages. The contents list ranges from a foreign newspaper leader on the new Russian manifesto to the launch of the Prince Royal in 1610.

Readers also find notes on the Ormulum, the legend of the Seven Sisters, and replies on subjects as varied as Welsh consonants, the screw propeller, and Shelley's Prometheus Unbound. The mix shows how Victorian readers traded facts, asked for help, and corrected one another in print. For anyone tracing a word, a family, or an old custom, the issue is a window onto mid-nineteenth-century antiquarian conversation.
31690-notes-and-queries-number-239-may-2:
Notes and Queries, number 239, for Saturday, May 27, 1854, presents itself as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, credited to Captain Cuttle, bids the reader to make a note when a thing is found. The number sold for fourpence, fivepence for the stamped edition.

Its notes include reprints of early Bibles by the Reverend R. Hooper, the marriage licence of John Gower the poet, a note on Aska or Asca, legends of the county Clare, and archaic words. Minor notes take up inscriptions on buildings, epitaphs, and numbers. The issue shows the journal's work of query, answer, and shared note-taking.
31885-bible-myths-and-their-parallels-in:
T. W. Doane's Bible Myths and Their Parallels in Other Religions, in its seventh edition with numerous illustrations, compares myths and miracles of the Old and New Testaments with those of ancient heathen nations. It also considers their origin and meaning. Its epigraph, from Professor Max Müller, holds that he who knows only one religion knows none.

Doane says the material was first accumulated for his private use. Most of what it holds can be found spread across hundreds of old and new volumes, yet no earlier work had followed these myths alone as its own book. Readers get a pioneering comparative work, arguing that Bible stories parallel older myths, written for readers willing to follow evidence across cultures.
32423-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with Coucy-le-Château, a northern French village, and runs through entries in the C range. Its index pages list subjects as varied as Cranbrook, Crane, Croatia-Slavonia, Crocodile, and Crockett, alongside legal and historical entries such as Council, Count, and Covenant. Each article gives the concise, sourced treatment that made the eleventh edition a standard reference.

Readers will find biography, geography, science, and history side by side, from artists and soldiers to animals, places, and institutions. The text preserves the edition's spelling, cross-references, and scholarly tone, with transcribers' notes on symbols and corrections. It works as a browsable reference volume and as a record of knowledge as it stood in the early twentieth century.
32807-freehold-land-societies-their-hist:
J. Ewing Ritchie explains the Freehold Land Movement in this pamphlet, published by William Tweedie in 1853 at twopence. The pages were reprinted from the Weekly News and Chronicle, the paper that called itself the organ of the movement.

Ritchie tells what the societies are, what they have done, and what they seek to do. Born of a working man, the movement offers working men independence, wealth, and political power. Members save together to buy land, and a forty-shilling freehold entitles a man to vote for the county. Ritchie weighs the scheme as an investment, a moral school, and a political force.
33631-the-story-of-a-strange-career-bein:
Edited by Stanley Waterloo, this 1902 volume presents itself as the authentic autobiography of a convict, and its career is indeed strange. The narrator, of an old New York family on his mother's side and a Dublin-born father, goes to sea young. He whales in the South Pacific, serves in Her Majesty's service, endures the cat-o'-nine-tails, and escapes. He survives as the sport of the waves.

Later chapters carry him through the New York draft riots, service as an acting ensign in the United States Navy, blockade running, prisoner-of-war life in Libby Prison, Fort Fisher, and Haiti. Later chapters also carry finally westward after leaving the sea. The narrative mixes adventure with prison experience, offering a picaresque life told in the first person. Readers should take its claim of authenticity as the book's own framing, not as settled fact.
34175-domestic-animals-history-and-descr:
R. L. Allen wrote this history and description of domestic animals, published in New York in 1865 by Orange Judd, entered under copyright in 1847. Allen, author of a Compend of American Agriculture, treats the horse, mule, cattle, sheep, swine, poultry, and farm dogs. He gives directions for management, breeding, crossing, rearing, feeding, and preparation for a profitable market. Farmers learn to keep stock healthy, raise young well, and sell at a gain.

Diseases and remedies follow, with full directions for managing the dairy. Allen writes for farmers who want sound, practical knowledge. The book remains a useful record of nineteenth-century American farming practice.
4675-the-sea-witch-or-the-african-quadro:
Lieutenant Murray wrote The Sea-Witch, or The African Quadroon, as a story of the slave coast, published at New York with other short tales bound in. Its contents run from Outward Bound and Captain Will Ratlin, through the gale, Bramble Park, the naval officer, and the wreck, to the Sea Witch herself and the quadroon. An attack, a duel, hues of love, a conflict, and a trial follow.

Later chapters add brothers, an escape, cannibals, a poisoned barb, and a denouement. Murray's preface asks readers not to take the book as a pro-slavery or anti-slavery tale, since slavery enters only where plot and locality require it. Readers get a sea adventure of its day, with wreck, pursuit, and romance on the African coast, plus extra stories by other hands in the same volume.
4678-lives-of-the-english-poets-gay-thom:
Samuel Johnson's Lives of the English Poets appears here in a volume covering Gay, Thomson, Young, Gray, and others, transcribed from the 1889 Cassell edition. The introduction says this volume records twenty lives, of which only Edward Young's is treated at length. It completes the edition of Johnson's Lives, from which only a few of the briefest and least important lives have been omitted.

The eldest poets discussed are Samuel Garth, Charles Montague, Lord Halifax, and William King, born in 1660 to 1663. Next come Ambrose Philips, friend of Addison, and Nicholas Rowe, dramatist and first editor of Shakespeare after the four folios, born in 1671 and 1673. Isaac Watts follows, born in 1674, then Thomas Parnell, born in 1679, nearly of like age with Young, born in 1681. Readers get Johnson's sharp, compact biographies, rich in judgement.
5263-the-girl-scout-pioneers-or-winning-:
Lillian C. Garis's Girl Scout Pioneers follows a troop of Girl Scouts working to win their first badge, here called the first B. C. Chapters move from girls and girls and woodland thrills through a noble deed undone, paths dividing, a friendly enemy, a novel jail. Tenderfoot adventures follow, toward a clue to the missing and a tribute of roses.

Garis, author of several Girl Scout books, writes cheerful stories of camping, teamwork, and pluck. The book offers young readers an early portrait of the Girl Scouts in action, with mysteries, woodland magic. The flying squadron carries the troop toward its goal.
6267-the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-e:
A quiet valley village, once a river bed in an age when the Thames flowed into the Seine, opens a novel that will travel to Cairo and back across fifty years. David Claridge leaves Hamley under a call, Faith waits and writes, Nahoum schemes in palaces, and Hylda seeks answers in bazaars. Six books carry the tale from a spirit moved and gates of the world through jehads, debts, desert struggles, and a loom of destiny.

Read whole, the novel joins an English Quaker household to Egyptian power, as David faces Kaid and Nahoum in palace rooms and Faith holds Hamley steady. Letters, compacts, and secrets bind the two worlds, and old wrongs return in desert and court alike. Parker writes a long romance of conscience and empire, where a village boy's calling reshapes a kingdom and costs him nearly everything he loves.
6868-why-and-how-a-hand-book-for-the-use:
Addie Chisholm, president of the Ontario Women's Christian Temperance Union, writes Why and How as a handbook for Canadian WCTU unions. Chapters run from suffering and awakening to organization and work, the Canadian union, why women should work, and how women may work. Forming a union, questions and answers, young women's work, and a dream follow, with a constitution and order of business.

Chisholm opens on woman's capacity for suffering through all past years and lands, and turns that suffering into a call to organize. Her tone is earnest and practical. Why and How is a clear, historic guide to temperance organizing by Canadian women.
7521-the-history-of-education-educationa:
Ellwood P. Cubberley, professor of education at Stanford University, built this history from his own teaching. Twenty-two years before, on entering Stanford, he was given the history of education to teach. He found he must construct a syllabus of lectures that would let him teach the subject as a living story. The syllabus grew, through a second edition, into this textbook, with a companion volume of readings.

Cubberley's argument is in his subtitle: educational practice and progress considered as a phase of the development and spread of Western civilization. Schools, he shows, did not grow in isolation; they grew with churches, states, and cities. The book, dedicated to his wife, thirty years his best companion in work and play, remains a classic university history of education.
7924-american-historical-and-literary-cu: This file stands for the whole second series of John Jay Smith's American Historical and Literary Antiquities, dated 1860, in one linked index volume. It is not a book to read through. Like its companion parts, it holds an editor's note explaining that the series is illustrations and page images, with little text that scanning could capture. Follow the note's links to the HTML editions and the index of all 22 volumes.
9294-the-exploring-expedition-to-the-roc:
Brevet Colonel John Charles Frémont wrote this narrative of his exploring expedition to the Rocky Mountains, Oregon, and California, here in its fifteenth thousand printing of 1852. A description of California's physical geography follows, with recent notices of the gold region from the latest sources. Frémont traveled by order of the United States government.

His preface calls the work the best yet to interest the American public, by a man eminently qualified for the task. Mountains, rivers, and gold fields unfold in his observations. The book remains a landmark of western exploration, and a first-hand account of a continent opening.
a-thief-in-the-night-further-adventures-:
A Thief in the Night, subtitled Further Adventures of A J Raffles, Cricketer and Cracksman, is a 1905 story collection by E W Hornung. It was the third book in the Raffles series and the final collection of short stories Hornung devoted to his gentleman thief. Raffles, the England cricketer who burgles the houses that host him, returns here with Bunny Manders at his side.

These last stories complete the short fiction of the series, after which the saga's shape was set. Readers get the established pleasure in its final form: society crime planned like sport, and friendship tested by shared risk. This edition presents the collection unabridged and illustrated, as a capstone to the cracksman's short adventures.
american-historical-and-literary-curiosi: John Jay Smith's complete second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities gathers the whole later sequence of illustrated antiquities in one place. Like its parts, the work is chiefly plates and page images, and the editor's note explains why the text file is partial, directing readers to HTML. As a complete set, it offers a broad visual record of American history and letters.
bank-of-the-manhattan-company-chartered-:
An anonymous corporate history celebrates the Bank of the Manhattan Company, chartered in 1799 and housed at 40 Wall Street. The present office, built jointly in 1884 with the Merchants' National Bank, fronts the volume. Origin, history, and progress are its announced themes, told as a progressive commercial bank's life story.

Early pages record the committee of by-laws devising a common seal on the eighth of May 1799: Oceanus, a sea god, pours water from an urn into a river. The watery emblem betrays the company's birth as a waterworks venture that also banked, Aaron Burr's famous double charter. Ledgers, presidents, and Wall Street addresses carry the tale forward, in the proud, illustrated manner of bank anniversary publications meant for customers and correspondents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-washington-d-:
Washington is the capital of the United States, on the Potomac's left bank 108 miles from Chesapeake Bay. Its district was originally ten miles square, reduced by Alexandria County's retrocession to Virginia in 1846 to about sixty square miles. The 1910 census counted 331,069 people, wholly urban, the county organization abolished in 1874, city and district now coextensive, with farmland valued chiefly as potential residence property.

No permanent seat existed until the Constitution empowered Congress to exercise exclusive jurisdiction over a district, by state cession, as the government's seat. Sessions were held in various places, chiefly Philadelphia, amid much sectional jealousy over rival sites. Later sections follow the city's Catholic history, including Father Matthews's parish, whose assistants included Father Pise, chaplain of the Senate in 1832 to 1833. Its parishioners included Chief Justice Taney, L'Enfant, planner of the city, Hoban, architect of the White House, and the first mayor, Robert Brent.
doe-osti-17084199-simulation-and-charact:
Wayne Witzel, Carolyn Mayer, and five Sandia colleagues present HERD, a framework for estimating how often quantum error correcting codes fail, in report SAND2026-26879R printed September 2026. Such codes protect quantum computers from noise, but their failure rates at working levels are so low that plain simulation rarely sees a failure to count.

HERD first builds a graph of harmful fault patterns that slip past detection, called BUFILOs in the report. It then samples the dangerous fault sets drawn from that graph to estimate logical failure rates without needing a specific decoder. Work centers on rotated surface codes under standard circuit noise, with checks against Monte Carlo and other rare event methods for speed and memory.
doe-osti-17116340-photovoltaic-operating:
Andy Walker and Jal Desai of the National Laboratory of the Rockies extend a solar plant upkeep cost model, in report NLR/TP-7A40-98313 dated September 2026. Adam Shinn of kWh Analytics and two more authors joined them. The update covers storm damage and insurance. Owners need yearly cost figures that include rare but costly hail and wind losses, not just routine care.

Weather hazard data from federal sources give local event size and frequency. A damage curve turns hazard strength into a share of broken panels. Curve fitting and worked examples show how damage cost is found. One example uses thicker glass as a hardening step. The last step folds in insurance terms, so owners can weigh cover against repair bills.
doe-osti-2584362-pnnl-dose-per-unit-rele:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory's dose factor compendium, by Sandra F. Snyder, Tristan R. Hay, and John M. Barnett in August 2025, supplies the numbers behind the lab's air emissions compliance. For each radionuclide, a dose-per-unit-release factor converts a quantity emitted into the dose a member of the public could receive. Multiply by a proposed source's potential emissions and you have its potential-to-emit dose, the figure regulators judge.

The factors are computed with the EPA's CAP88-PC code for the Richland and Sequim campuses, with location adjustment factors for specific facilities. The document has lived through revisions since 2008, absorbing new code versions, fresh meteorological data, and a 100-year buildup assumption for continuous operation. Surrogate factors cover nuclides the code lacks. Dry as it reads, this is load-bearing paperwork: every notice of construction for a PNNL building with radioactive emissions stands on these tables.
doe-osti-2588689-advancing-understanding:
Zhihong Lin's final report for award DE-SC0021316, covering September 2020 through August 2025, tackles fast-ion driven instabilities in NSTX-U, the spherical tokamak at Princeton. Fast ions from heating beams can excite waves that then throw the fast ions out, degrading heating and confinement. Predicting that loop is the project's business.

The approach pairs experiment with the global gyrokinetic code GTC. Physics models inside GTC were validated against NSTX-U measurements of the instabilities and the anomalous transport they cause. Verification ran alongside: a fully kinetic ion model for electromagnetic simulation of high-frequency waves was checked against analytic dispersion relations. Linear simulations of the ion Bernstein wave and ion cyclotron emission matched theory in cylindrical geometry. The five-year award closes with a stronger predictive capability for spherical tokamak design, where fast-ion effects can make or break performance.
doe-osti-2997793-attempting-to-develop-t:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory final report ORNL/TM-2025/4255, by Michael Kesler, Michael Thompson, Max Neveau, and co-authors, dated October 2025, closes cooperative project NFE-20-08213 on a low-cost metal printing nozzle. The approach feeds aluminum wire through an induction-heated electromagnetic nozzle mounted on a computer-controlled machine, melting metal only at the tip. Partners included the University of Tennessee and Hybrid Manufacturing Technologies.

Simulation work set the design numbers: wire enters at 30 degrees Celsius and leaves at 777 degrees, driven at 48 volts with feed rates of 7 to 10 millimeters per second. An energy balance analysis over those cases fixed the essential parameters for the induction system. The project goal, stated in its title, is the most cost-effective metal printing route the team can reach through industrial adoption. The filing records the design basis for that push.
doe-osti-2998013-improvement-and-verific:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/NSE-25/82, by Hansol Park and Changho Lee, improves how the Griffin reactor code builds its own nuclear data during a run. Griffin serves reactors fueled with TRISO particles, whose layered kernels shield themselves from neutrons in ways simple tables miss. Online cross-section generation recomputes those data as conditions change, and this report verifies the upgrade, with an errata sheet correcting the first printing in October 2025.

The method slows neutrons in two stages and corrects for particles shadowing each other through the Dancoff factor, now computed by category with a Bell function weighting. Non-fuel resonances get their own treatment, including a Tone method option. A Bondarenko iteration consumes the assembled tables to produce effective cross sections per isotope and energy group. Analysts gain a checked, faster path from raw data to core answers.
doe-osti-2998856-ion-pair-proton-exchang: Kotaro Sasaki's Brookhaven National Laboratory sheet BNL-229006-2025-FORE, dated September 2025, is a short abstract for a cooperative research agreement, CRADA C-24-13, with Advent Technologies. The project aims to build a high-temperature proton exchange membrane fuel cell prototype fit for heavy-duty trucks. It would join Los Alamos ion-pair membrane work with Brookhaven catalyst work. Target cells must run across a range of heat and humidity, accept low-grade or pure hydrogen, and resist dirty air.
doe-osti-2999866-scoping-study-of-integr:
Jian Sun, Yanfei Li, Kashif Nawaz and co-workers at Oak Ridge National Laboratory scope a heating idea in ORNL/TM-2024/3521, a CRADA final report dated October 2025. Cold regions need strong heating, and ground-source heat pumps sip steady warmth from below ground. Many rural homes already own a water well. The study asks whether one well can serve both water supply and heat pump duty, using carbon dioxide as the working fluid.

Mathematical models and system designs were worked out for homes. Of the well types reviewed, artesian, bedrock, drilled and collector wells suit the pairing, offering strong flow, clean water, stable temperatures and low environmental impact. Four heat pump designs were compared. Units using R-410A refrigerant proved more efficient than the carbon dioxide units. The carbon dioxide systems still win on cleanliness and energy security grounds, the authors note, since the gas is not a synthetic pollutant.
doe-osti-3002038-attempting-to-develop-t:
Michael Kesler, Michael Thompson, Max Neveau, Adrian Sabau, and Wenjun Ge of Oak Ridge close out CRADA project NFE-20-08213 in ORNL/TM-2025/4255, dated October 2025. Their partners were the University of Tennessee and HMT. The goal was a cheaper way to 3D print metal. Their approach feeds metal wire through a high-temperature electromagnetic nozzle tied into computer-controlled machining.

Much of the work models induction heating of aluminum alloy wire. A one-dimensional model predicts wire temperature, melting, the power each coil section needs, and coil spacing for solid, semi-solid, and liquid zones. Simulations pointed to design changes, such as moving an insulator closer to the susceptor to cut heat loss. The team also suggests pairing the physics model with machine learning next.
doe-osti-3003814-staged-z-pinch-modeling:
Drew Higginson of Lawrence Livermore and Hafiz Ur Rahman of Magneto-Inertial Fusion Technologies close CRADA TC02390 in report LLNL-TR-2013183, dated July 18, 2023. Technical work ended in January 2023. The project modeled staged Z-pinch devices, which crush a plasma target with magnetic pressure to reach fusion conditions. Two simulation codes did the modeling.

Hydra, Livermore's radiation-hydrodynamics code, and Chicago, a three-dimensional electromagnetic particle-in-cell code, were both brought to bear on the partner's staged Z-pinch targets. The Energy Department's INFUSE program sponsored the work, with 200,000 dollars of program funding plus in-kind contributions. Background patents cover Z-pinch neutron production and staged designs aimed at net energy. CRADA final reports like this one are mostly administrative, but they fix the public record of the collaboration.
doe-osti-3006483-the-risk-assessment-inf:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4312, dated November 2025, is Volume VII of the Risk Assessment Information System compendium of ecological screening benchmarks for chemicals and radionuclides. Five authors are listed: Janou S. Milligan, Debra J. Stewart, Fredrick G. Dolislager, Katie A. Noto, and Karessa L. Manning. This volume covers chemicals in marine sediment. The compendium gives screening values that assessors compare against measured contaminant levels when judging ecological risk at cleanup and industrial sites.

The bulk of the volume is benchmark tables with numbered footnotes. Many values are formulas rather than fixed numbers: several entries compute a benchmark from water hardness or pH through exponential expressions, with hardness expressed as milligrams per liter of calcium carbonate. The 2025 edition updates the running RAIS reference set.
doe-osti-3006489-the-risk-assessment-inf:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4306, dated November 2025, is Volume I of the Risk Assessment Information System compendium of ecological screening benchmarks for chemicals and radionuclides. Five authors are listed: Janou S. Milligan, Debra J. Stewart, Fredrick G. Dolislager, Katie A. Noto, and Karessa L. Manning. This volume carries the main text, radionuclide benchmarks for all media, and chemical benchmarks for air and biota.

Early chapters explain the ecological benchmarks tool: how to select benchmark sources, choose media, pick contaminants, retrieve results, and review and export them. Chemical sources are catalogued next. The bulk of the book is tables with numbered footnotes, many giving formulas keyed to hardness or pH rather than fixed values. A closing radionuclide footnote set explains inclusions such as barium-137 and yttrium-90, plus minimum screening level rules.
doe-osti-3010843-controlling-interfacial:
Final scientific report for DOE award DE-SC0021189, by Justin Sambur of Colorado State University, covers hot-carrier energy conversion in two-dimensional semiconductors. Ordinary solar cells waste photon energy above the band gap as heat within trillionths of a second; beating the roughly 33 percent Shockley-Queisser limit means catching carriers before they cool.

Monolayer molybdenum disulfide photoelectrodes, about three atomic layers thick, shorten the escape route to almost nothing. Electrochemical microscopy and ultrafast spectroscopy directly showed hot carriers transferring into the liquid electrolyte fast enough to compete with cooling, in working liquid junction cells. The project also mapped the design rules: how interfacial energetics and transfer rates must be tuned against cooling rates.
doe-osti-3011895-combined-algae-processi:
Combined algae processing is reviewed as a route to algal fuels and coproducts in a white paper by Matthew Wiatrowski, Bruno Klein, Lieve Laurens, and Ryan Davis. All four authors work at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. The approach fractionates microalgae biomass and converts each constituent stream. Commercialisation barriers for algal biofuels frame the discussion.

Design cases trace yields across a decade of work. A 2014 high lipid design gave 141 gasoline gallon equivalents per ton with no coproducts. The 2030 state of technology targets sit near 72 to 73 with polyurethane coproducts. Either a carboxylic acid or a butanediol pathway reaches those figures. A 2023 industry case study reached 81 with the acid pathway.
doe-osti-3013455-comparative-assessment-:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2025/4326, by M. D. Shah, D. Hartanto, and K. Donnelly, dated January 2026, compares what happens if saboteurs deliberately breach different microreactors. Microreactor developers want smaller security forces and emergency planning zones, leaning on robust fuel and passive safety instead. That trade raises the sabotage question this study answers with consequence modeling rather than opinion.

Five designs, each rated at 30 megawatts thermal, were tested on paper: pressurized water, sodium fast, high-temperature helium prismatic, heat pipe, and molten salt cooled units. Two sabotage accidents were defined per design, with set fission product release fractions. Doses were checked against the criterion of 25 rem over the first two hours at the site boundary, informing how large each design's emergency planning zone must be.
doe-osti-3013586-probing-the-flavor-depe:
Heather Gray of the University of California, Berkeley, wrote this final report for Early Career award DE-SC0021046, covering September 2020 to August 2025. Working in the ATLAS experiment at CERN, Gray's program chased the Higgs boson's coupling to charm quarks, a measurement that tests whether the Higgs treats each particle flavor as theory predicts. The path ran through better charm-jet identification.

The team contributed to ATLAS's graph neural network tagger GN2. At 70 percent b-tagging efficiency, GN2 reaches charm-jet rejection near 45 and light-jet rejection near 2200, better than four times the early Run 3 performance. A soft-electron tagging module they built improved charm and light rejection by about 15 percent at fixed efficiency. Precision measurements of electroweak production with charm rounded out the program.
doe-osti-3013834-center-for-bio-inspired:
Samuel Stupp's final report closes the Center for Bio-Inspired Energy Science. The center was an Energy Frontier Research Center. It built materials and systems modeled on biology to convert and store energy. The report focuses on the final funding cycle, 2022 to 2024, which extended five strategic tasks. Soft matter, gels, fibers, and molecular assemblies are the center's working materials.

One task made artificial muscles from spiropyran hydrogels embedded with nickel nanowires. The muscles walk in magnetic fields and contract under light. Supramolecular nanofibers turned out to strengthen both the gel and its photo-response. Other tasks covered light harvesting, charge transport, and catalysis with bio-inspired designs. The summary argues that soft materials can perform energy functions once reserved for hard crystals, with gentler chemistry.
doe-osti-3018741-deliberate-motion-analy:
Luke J Gilbert, JR Russell, Dave Novick, and Dan Small of Sandia, with Peter Blemel and Joel Gloetzner of Management Sciences Inc, wrote SAND2026-16255R in January 2026. The threat is small drones flown without radio control. Waypoint and vision-guided drones emit nothing for detectors to hear. Deliberate Motion Analytics looks for them by movement instead. The project applied the algorithm to counter-UAS sensor fusion. A market survey and testbed came first, stocked with systems such as the Magos AR-300 and EchoDyne radar.

Trials ran from a test area with the drone trailer as launch point. Sensors covered azimuthal ranges up to 130 degrees. The fusion question is practical: which sensor combinations catch a quiet drone soon enough to matter? Threats named in the summary include explosives delivery and covert surveillance. For site security teams, the report prices a detection approach aimed at the drones that RF gear misses.
doe-osti-3021565-manufacturing-full-scal:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-21495, by Alex Murokh, Paul Carrier, and Evgenya Ivanovna Simakov, issued March 2, 2026, is a manufacturing handbook for full-scale, high-gradient copper accelerator structures. These radio-frequency structures, built from precision-machined copper disks, must be joined without ruining their shape or their vacuum-tight surfaces. The report compares the conventional route, hydrogen furnace brazing, with electron beam welding and allied processes.

Sections cover feedstock selection, machining precision versus the cost of manual tuning, metrology, chemical cleaning, and capital and staffing needs. Electron beam welding details include beam deflection patterns that shape the weld pool, and multi-pool methods that preheat and then smooth the weld crown in the same pass. The goal is a production path for meter-scale structures that holds the tolerances accelerator physics demands.
doe-osti-3021934-quantifying-the-operati:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory abbreviated final report LLNL-TR-2011985, by Domingo Colon, dated March 2026, reports LDRD feasibility study 25-FS-027 on reading cyber events from wireless data. Network defenders drown in alerts; this study asked whether change-detection algorithms Livermore built for wired enterprise data could extract value from passively collected radio-frequency and wireless network traffic instead.

The study built an interpretable clustering method for wireless device behavior and tested it on known device populations. Five features proved sufficient to capture how wireless access points behave, accurately enough to predict device type and function. Results depended on data density and collection window length, which set how sharply cluster boundaries resolve. Applied to security datasets, the approach supports behavioral profiling, drift detection, and real-time anomaly alerts. The findings are already shaping follow-on proposals, including a possible larger effort in fiscal year 2026.
doe-osti-3022263-energy-baseline-assessm:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-6A20-97088, by Robin Burton, builds the energy baseline for a community energy plan in the Wai'anae moku, the leeward district of O'ahu, Hawai'i. It documents how the community uses energy today, what it pays, and where the system is fragile, giving local planners and residents a shared factual starting point for decisions.

Project considerations grow out of that baseline. Goals include a network of resilience hubs across the moku by 2030, each able to keep serving residents through outages. The report examines hybrid microgrids under Hawaiian Electric's tariff model. It also describes how the lab, with Sandia National Laboratories, helped evaluate microgrid sites by criticality, meaning closeness to emergency facilities, and by vulnerability to natural hazards.
doe-osti-3022996-level-2-milestone-9009-:
Kathryn Mohror, Brian Behlendorf, and Matthew LeGendre of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report a finished Level-2 milestone, number 9009, in June 2025. Report LLNL-TR-2007205 covers two capabilities brought up on El Capitan: the Flux workload manager and Rabbit, the machine's fast storage tier. Big supercomputers need software that hands out computing resources and moves data without wasting either.

Flux is described as a next-generation resource and job manager built for extreme scale. Each job runs inside its own instance of the manager, which allows nested scheduling and fine control over resources. The milestone format is plain: what was promised, what was built, and how the pieces behave on the real machine.
doe-osti-3023259-a-scalable-test-bed-for:
Chirag Birla, David Bergman, Michael Charumaneeroj, and colleagues at Brookhaven National Laboratory describe a test-bed for direct current current transformers in technical note BNL-229533-2026-TECH, dated March 2026. These transformers measure beam current at light sources such as NSLS-II, and each unit needs functional testing and characterization. Doing that by hand is slow, so the note presents a scalable automated rig.

Measurement data are validated in real time while tests run. The automation program was written in Python, using pyvisa for instrument control and pandas, matplotlib, and openpyxl for analysis and processing. Sections walk through the test setup and method, the design flow, results, and closing comments, with the amplifier and terminal wiring shown in a setup figure.
doe-osti-3029153-courage-kazr-b1-process:
Min Deng of Brookhaven National Laboratory, Adam Theisen of Argonne, and Marquette Rocque, A Matthews, E Schuman of Pacific Northwest, with Z Zhu. They document radar data processing for the CoURAGE campaign in DOE/SC-ARM-TR-331, dated March 2026. The instrument is the KAZR, a Ka-band cloud radar, and the b1 product is its corrected, calibrated datastream. Rain on the radar's own dome is the villain of this particular story.

Calibration of the general mode leans on disdrometer observations at the ground, matched to the radar's shallow precipitation and near-surface returns. An explicit correction handles wet radome attenuation, the signal loss from a thin water film on the dome, which otherwise bends reflectivity readings with rain rate. The method follows Deng and colleagues, 2024, and accounts for the two-way path of the radar pulse through the film.
doe-osti-3030065-cyber-halo-innovation-r:
Penny McKenzie, Lisa Campbell, Ann Wright-Mockler, and colleagues at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory wrote this 2026 handbook for the Cyber Halo Innovation Research Program, report PNNL-39147. CHIRP trains students for space cybersecurity work. It serves the United States Space Force Space Systems Command, which needs staff who can guard satellites and ground systems. The handbook lays out how the program recruits, teaches, and places its students.

Cohorts work on real command needs with faculty advisors and mentors, then hand their projects to the next group. A shared store holds summaries of past work, tools, code, and lessons, so new students build on old results instead of starting over. Once a year, command leaders and program staff review what the pipeline delivered, where it fell short, and what to stress next.
doe-osti-3364919-interregional-transmiss:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-6A40-99604 studies how neighboring grid regions coordinate operations across their seams. Yonghong Chen, Jose Daniel Lara, Haotian Chen, Matthew Bossart, Sebastian Manrique Machado, and Jarrad Wright wrote it. When two markets share a congested line, uncoordinated dispatch wastes capacity. Market-to-market coordination lets the regions redispatch together against shared constraints.

The study builds a multistage framework that follows decisions from day-ahead scheduling into real time. Models pass interchange schedules and loop flow data between stages, and generation outages with reserve responses can be defined per area. Post-reserve transmission limits are enforced after each outage case. The Sienna simulation tools implement the framework. Results aim to show grid operators what tighter seam coordination is worth in practice.
doe-osti-3365002-evaluation-of-damage-in:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report PNNL-38233, by S. W. Glass, J. R. Tedeschi, M. Elen, M. Taufique, and L. S. Fifield with J. A. Farber and A. Kaforey of Idaho National Laboratory, tests whether machine learning can spot damage in medium voltage cable. The September 2025 work, under the Light Water Reactor Sustainability Program, ran on the ARENA cable test bed. Reflectometry traces from damaged and sound cables look nearly identical to the eye.

The test cable ran 50 feet with a 20-foot leader, and both frequency domain and spread spectrum reflectometry were recorded through a clamp-on coupler. Damage cases were compared against undamaged baselines trace by trace. Because visual differences stay subtle, the team fed the traces to learning algorithms to find patterns humans miss. Success would give plant staff a non-destructive way to grade aging cable in place.
doe-osti-3365072-continuous-energy-verif:
Report LA-UR-26-23580 from Los Alamos National Laboratory, by Avneet Sood and issued May 4, 2026, verifies the MCNP radiation transport code against textbook criticality benchmarks. The benchmarks are one-group spheres and slabs whose critical sizes are known analytically as a function of a single multiplication parameter. If MCNP's continuous-energy machinery is sound, it should reproduce criticality exactly for these simple systems.

Pseudo-isotope cross sections held transport and scattering fixed while the neutron yield was tuned to each benchmark case. Calculations ran with the KCODE criticality option and large particle populations. Slab results stayed within about 1.5 standard deviations of the exact answer across all cases, with deviations balanced in sign and no drift with the parameter. Sphere results matched the same way, confirming the implementation for both geometries.
doe-osti-3365152-glovebox-cfd-analysis-l:
At Los Alamos National Laboratory, report LA-UR-26-24343 by Nathan Wolff models air movement inside a glovebox with the Ansys Fluent 2025 R1 simulation code. Gloveboxes hold hazardous material work, and their ventilation must sweep humidity and contaminants toward the exhaust without dead zones. The study treats the low-flow, laminar regime, where air glides in smooth layers instead of tumbling turbulently.

The final setup uses a mass flow inlet and pressure outlet. Inlet flow was 0.0022 kilograms per second, about 5 cubic feet per minute, at Los Alamos conditions: 7,300 feet elevation, 20 degrees Celsius, and 78 kilopascals pressure. Solver options meant for transient problems were switched off to keep the steady-state solution clean. Humidity transport rides on the flow field, showing where moist air lingers in the box.
doe-osti-3365890-manufacturing-full-scal:
A RadiaBeam Technologies report for the DOE ARDAP program, contract DE-SC0023618, by R. Agustsson, P. Carriere, S. Kutsaev, A. Murokh, and M. Ruelas with E. Simakov of Los Alamos, examines electron beam welding as the way to build high-gradient copper accelerators at full scale. Thousands of linacs are built yearly, but few run at high gradient, largely because such structures are costly and hard to manufacture.

Welding split copper structures with an electron beam promises precision joints without brazing furnaces. A case study tests the approach against the C3 accelerator structure design. Equipment chapters weigh internal against external electron guns: high-voltage guns above 60 kilovolts focus tighter and reach farther, while internal guns risk contamination. The report closes with establishing and operating a production facility, moving the method from studies to a working line.
doe-osti-3367393-2026-innovating-the-gas:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory's report ORNL/TM-2026/4585 records the May 2026 Innovating the Gas Turbine Supply Chain workshop, convened by Edgar Lara-Curzio's directorate. Gas turbines sit at the center of grid reliability plans, yet their supply chains, from superalloy castings to hot-section coatings, are thin and slow. The workshop gathered manufacturers, researchers, and government staff to map the bottlenecks.

Participants pressed for faster ways to screen candidate materials so scarce test resources go to the most promising options. Combined-effects testing, exposing materials to corrosion, erosion, thermal fatigue, and stress at once, was judged essential but hard to run at scale, and better in situ diagnostics during testing drew equal support. The proceedings preserve the industry's own diagnosis of its constraints.
doe-osti-3375448-comparing-synthetic-rou:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-25231, issued June 24, 2026, compares how well alternate APO resin variants can be made and how they take heat. Zoey R. Coleman and Makena K. Vetter head a seven-person team. APO is a bismaleimide base resin for high-performance foams. The legacy form links its bridge through sulfur. The team built eleven variants that swap that bridge atom or stiffen the frame.

Bond lengths tell much of the story. The carbon-sulfur bond in legacy APO is long. Carbon-oxygen bonds in the new forms run near 1.36 angstroms. Carbon-nitrogen bonds run a touch longer. Shorter bonds pack tighter and pull harder, so the new forms may replace the old. Heat tests back the split. One trans-butene form melts at 131 and 156 degrees. The legacy resin melts at 126 and 144.
doe-osti-3376229-electrochemical-evaluat:
A final INFUSE report for award DE-SC0024473, dated September 30, 2025, covers a UC Berkeley study of hydrogen in FLiBe salt. Raluca O. Scarlat and Guanyu Su led the campus work. Caroline Sorensen Barthen of Commonwealth Fusion Systems was the company partner. FLiBe is the molten salt picked to breed tritium in the ARC fusion plant. Two traits govern how tritium moves through it: how much dissolves, and how fast it diffuses.

Those traits are poorly pinned down. Past solubility reads spread across three orders of magnitude. Their heat trends clash as well. The team built an electrochemical method to measure both traits in one setup. Tiny disk and wire electrodes take a voltage step, and the current decay tells the tale. Model runs check the fit. For a wire of 38.1 microns, the simulated current settled to the same steady state as the analytic path after about one thousand seconds.
doe-osti-3376522-prioritizing-uncertaint:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-22699, printed in June 2026, ranks the unknowns in a risk model for hydrogen trains after a crash. Dusty Brooks, Benjamin B. Schroeder, Qi Guo, and Brian D. Ehrhart wrote it. Hydrogen fuel adds new stakes to old rail hazards: derailments, collisions, and fires. A risk model built on shaky rates will mislead. The team set out to learn which input rates sway the answer most, so field data work can start there.

The report fits smooth curves to yearly event counts from rail records. Derailments, train-to-train hits, and train-to-other hits each get a gamma distribution. Freight fire and explosion rates take one too, with shape and scale values printed per case. Passenger cases are fit apart from freight. The ranked list tells modelers where a better count buys the most truth.
doe-osti-3376765-automation-of-solid-oxy:
A final report for Department of Energy award DE-EE0009622 closes a Cummins Electrified Power project on robot assembly of solid oxide electrolyzer cells. Todd Kobiela is the contact of record. The project ran from August 2022 to October 2023. These cells split water into hydrogen at high heat. Their parts are thin, brittle, and costly to scrap. Hand stacking is slow and uneven, so the team scoped machines to do the handling.

Work strands covered process, materials, in-line gauges, and automation trials. One fork in the road was the gripper. Plain electromagnets held too weakly, so a set grew heavy and bulky. That load would swamp the team's UR-10e test robot and crowd the parts rack. A second style, a fixed magnet with air-driven field control, won out. It grips magnetic alloy parts hard at low cost. Quotes for the full line went out to builders.
doe-osti-3425457-upgrading-biogas-throug:
Washington University in St. Louis closes award DE-EE0009771 with a final report on upgrading biogas inside anaerobic digesters. Zhen He led the project. The project ran from October 1, 2021 to January 31, 2026. Cornell, Argonne, Virginia Tech, and Anheuser-Busch partnered on the work.

Magnesium oxide pellets were tested for grabbing carbon dioxide from gas mixes. Breakthrough came much faster for methane than for carbon dioxide. The resulting selectivity was about 8 to 1, above the project target stated in the text. Turning carbon dioxide into biomethane in place would raise the fuel value of digester gas.
doe-osti-3682491-2026-innovating-the-gas:
A workshop on the gas turbine supply chain is recorded in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2026/4585, dated May 2026. Edgar Lara-Curzio is the named author and compiler. Plenary talks open the volume. One maps market signals, bottlenecks, and cost pressure across the chain. Another gives the maker's view, where parts stand out as the defining bottleneck. Large structural parts carry added risk from trade and geopolitics.

Breakout groups then worked six themes, from raw materials to workforce growth. Additive manufacturing runs through the talks as a lever for scarce parts. Standards and qualification steps decide how fast new routes can scale. Test capacity is a sore point: combined heat, corrosion, erosion, and stress tests are wanted but hard to run at scale. Groups also asked for better in-process sensors and for machine learning to screen candidate materials faster. Each session ends with gaps, roles, and named actions.
doe-osti-3685241-cyber-halo-innovation-r:
Pacific Northwest student research report, dated July 2026, sums up the Cyber Halo Innovation Research Program, called CHIRP. Penny McKenzie and Aubrie Kendall are the named authors of the programme analysis. Two student cohorts took part. The first sat at California State University San Bernardino, and the second at the University of Texas at El Paso. Topics all orbit cyber defence for space systems.

First-cohort work covered a space cyber test range and attack awareness. Later solo work took up post-quantum cryptography, AI for space security, and satellite intrusion spotting. One study used data provenance, the full history of a data item, to catch intruders. Its test bed paired a provenance capture tool with a known detection system. Results suggest provenance checks can spot advanced attacks that standard tools miss, at some added computing cost.
enoch-arden-c:
Alfred Tennyson's Enoch Arden volume of 1864 leads with its title poem. The sailor Enoch, shipwrecked for ten years, returns to find his wife remarried. He chooses silence over her happiness. Long lines of cliff and a mouldered church open his seaside village. Aylmer's Field and Sea Dreams, two more narrative poems of class and conscience, follow.

The miscellaneous section gives Tithonus, who begs release from endless age, the Northern Farmer speaking dialect, a welcome to Princess Alexandra, and experiments including a blank-verse Iliad specimen. Boadicea rages in galloping meter nearby. The volume marked Tennyson's popular height as laureate: narrative feeling, classical myth, and dialect character under one cover, bought by readers who rarely bought poetry.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AmericanScholar: In March 1967 a reader wrote to the editor of The American Scholar, the Phi Beta Kappa quarterly, in anger over John Kaplan's article in the Spring issue. The letter denounces Kaplan's piece as 'shameful, dishonorable and slanderously titled,' strong words for a scholarly journal's letters page. The author's name cannot be recovered from the text. The single letter survives as a sample of the fierce literary quarrels that the era's debates could start in respectable pages.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ArmyBehaviorCon: Government material filed under the heading Army Behavior Control makes up this file, released without a fuller description. The Army's behavior control work of the Cold War ran through places like Edgewood Arsenal, where soldiers were dosed with LSD and other compounds in secret tests. Programs of that kind later became public through congressional hearings and lawsuits brought by the test subjects. The file is kept as titled, a fragment of the record of those experiments.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-EdwardsDonCongr:
Researcher Harold Weisberg wrote to Congressman Don Edwards with a sharp charge. The 1975 hearings on FBI agent James Hosty, he said, had been stage-managed to cover the FBI's failures. Weisberg attached material to back his case, including names, addresses, and phone numbers that had been withheld.

The letter is a critic going over the heads of the Bureau to Congress. Edwards sat where oversight could bite, and Weisberg supplied him with the very details he said officials had kept back. It shows how assassination researchers used congressional allies to force hidden records into the open.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JencksClintonEv:
Justice William Brennan wrote the Supreme Court's opinion in the case of Clinton E. Jencks against the United States, decided June 3, 1957. Jencks was a labor organizer prosecuted with help from FBI informers. The Court ruled for his right to see the Bureau reports behind the testimony used against him.

The decision forced the government to open its files to the defense or drop its case. Congress answered within months with the Jencks Act, which still governs witness statements in federal trials. The opinion preserved here is the source of that rule, a landmark in the rights of the accused.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ThompsonWC_Thom: nsia-ThompsonWC Thompson W C: the declassified government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, preserved as released. An obscure item, complete. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ThomsonGeorgeC_: nsia-ThomsonGeorgeC Thomson George C: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-selected-cantos-of-e:
Ezra Pound spent fifty years building The Cantos, a vast poem of history, money, and myth. Selected Cantos gathers a shorter path through that work, running from the Fourth Canto of 1919 to the Pisan Cantos.

The Pisan poems were written while Pound was held in a cage in Italy after the Second World War, and many readers count them his finest work. A selection cannot hold the whole epic, but it shows the range: many voices, many languages, and a fierce argument about how societies rot and renew. The volume stands as a landmark of modernist poetry.
govdocs-archive_org-the-original-sources:
