W. St. Clair Tisdall, a missionary scholar, asked where the Quran's stories came from. The Original Sources of the Quran argues that many passages draw on pagan legends and on earlier Jewish and Christian scriptures.

Tisdall compares texts side by side, hunting for the earlier forms of names, tales, and teachings. His method is classic comparative source criticism, and his book became a standard work in that field. Modern scholars dispute parts of his case, but the volume still shows how the search for sources was done at its most confident.
hume-history-of-england-1860-part-c:
David Hume's History of England reaches Part C in the 1860 Virtue edition, the third of six parts. Hume, Scotland's great philosopher, issued the history between 1754 and 1762. In his lifetime it outsold his philosophy and set the pattern for English history writing.

The work covers the whole span from Caesar's invasion to the revolution of 1688. Hume's gift was balance: he gave each party its due and spared each party his irony. His sentences flow with a calm that hides deep judgment. Part C stands at the middle of the set, where the long story of the island gathers weight. The full history runs to seventy-one chapters.
lives-of-the-english-poets-gay-thomson-y:
Samuel Johnson's lives in this Cassell volume cover twenty poets. Cassell published the 1889 edition in London, Paris, and Melbourne. Only Edward Young's life receives full length treatment here. The introduction says brief, minor lives were omitted from the edition.

Garth, Halifax, and King were born between 1660 and 1663. Ambrose Philips, Nicholas Rowe, and Isaac Watts follow in age. John Gay, born 1688, stands near the sequence's end. James Thomson of The Seasons and John Dyer appear too. Thomas Parnell, born 1679, nearly matched Young's age exactly. William Somerville of The Chace arrived in 1692 afterward.
nasa-tm-19650019801-measurement-of-the-c:
Eugene J Manista and John W Sheldon at Lewis Research Center measured how strongly cesium atoms scatter off each other. Their letter, prepared in September 1964 for a physics journal, uses atomic beam methods. In those methods, a narrow stream of atoms crosses another stream, and the deflection is measured. The quantity found is called the total cross section.

Earlier workers had found an unusually large value for cesium. Interest was rising because cesium served in electronic devices that use hot gases. The authors set their new measurement beside the earlier one. Atomic data of this kind feed the design of those devices.
nasa-tm-19650027176-the-effect-of-gold-p:
S D Ebneter, in Marshall's Quality and Reliability Assurance Laboratory, wrote this October 15, 1965, memorandum on gold plating and solder. Electronic parts are often gold plated for protection. Those same parts must later be joined with solder. Ebneter asks what the gold layer does to the strength and quality of a soldered connection.

A plating that helps storage could hurt joining, if the two do not mix well. Flight hardware carries thousands of soldered joints. Weak joints are a classic source of failure in service. A laboratory study like this one gave assembly shops a factual base for their rules on plated parts.
nasa-tm-19670005569-technical-manual-bas:
Volume 5 of the Base Support Services Contractor technical manual was issued on April 1, 1966, at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The six-volume manual spells out what the contractor in charge of base support must do. This volume covers base utilities, their operation and maintenance.

The set's other volumes cover administration, preventive maintenance, roads and grounds, and heavy equipment. The catalog record describes this volume as procedures for maintaining the space center's base utilities. The hosted sample preserves the cover and notice pages, so the procedures themselves cannot be described in detail.
nasa-tm-19670009249-on-the-formation-of-:
B. Donn, T. P. Stecher, N. C. Wickramasinghe, and J. P. Hudson, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this paper on September 21, 1966. It asks how solid graphite grains can form inside the atmospheres of cool stars. Their answer rests on newly available data about how molecules balance against each other in stellar air.

The authors re-examined the Hoyle-Wickramasinghe condensation mechanism for carbon-rich N-type stars, now accounting for hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen. From published tables, free carbon pressure tops graphite's vapor pressure once a pulsating star cools below about twenty-four hundred degrees Kelvin. Grains then need seed particles to start growing, and only modest supersaturation is required on existing ions. Crystal growth runs fast at the available carbon pressures. Final grain size, they conclude, is set by how much carbon and how many seeds are present.
nasa-tm-19680025305-analysis-and-design-:
Heinz Erzberger of Ames Research Center presents state space methods for model following control systems in this paper. A model follower forces a real plant, such as an aircraft, to track a model's behavior. Designers must first know when perfect following is even possible.

Erzberger gives a test that decides when a linear plant's output can follow a model exactly using feedback. Two configurations are covered: implicit model following and real model following. Without disturbances, the conditions for perfect following are essentially the same for both. Earlier quadratic optimal control methods always produced a feedback law, but they left such design questions open. State space techniques address those questions directly.
nasa-tm-19690004981-experimental-investi:
Donald L. Bresnahan of Lewis Research Center tested a ten-degree conical turbojet plug nozzle in this report. The nozzle paired an iris primary throat with a translating outer shroud. Tests ran in a static facility and the 8-by-6-foot supersonic wind tunnel, covering Mach numbers from zero to 2.0.

Full-length plug efficiency stayed above ninety-six percent at most flight conditions. Subsonic cruise was the exception, where external flow effects grew significant. Shortening the plug cost little efficiency at supersonic cruise. At subsonic cruise, truncation losses were larger, especially for the shortest plug. Internal expansion was adjusted by sliding the shroud. The results suit supersonic cruise engine design work.
nasa-tm-19700008012-aerodynamic-investig:
Engineers at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland studied a set of four turbine vanes built for cooling research. The vanes formed a curved ring sector, called a cascade. The study measured how air moved through and past the vanes.

The team measured static and total pressures where the air left the cascade. They also took surface pressures at three points along each vane. Those surface readings matter because they help set vane metal temperatures in later heat tests. Tests ran on cool, low-pressure air at three exit speeds. The report states that the vane set showed acceptable air flow traits.
nasa-tm-19700019321-rotational-excitatio:
F. H. M. Faisal wrote this Goddard Space Flight Center preprint on rotational excitations of molecules. Faisal was a research associate working at Goddard on a fellowship, on leave from the Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission. His subject is what happens when atoms strike molecules and set them spinning faster.

Using first order semi-classical scattering theory, Faisal estimates the excitation cross-sections for nitrogen molecules hit by neon atoms. Cross-sections measure how likely such a hit is to spin the molecule up. He compares his figures with full quantum calculations already available. The working assumptions stay simple: straight-line paths for the heavy incoming atoms, and a solution worked out in closed form.
nasa-tm-19700024999-apollo-entry-summary:
L. D. Carrico Jr. of the McDonnell Douglas Astronautics Company led the team that prepared this Apollo entry summary. W. W. Hinton Jr. of the same firm and J. O. Rippey of the Manned Spacecraft Center also took part. The document covers the C prime mission.

An entry summary gathers the facts a crew needs for the return through Earth's air. This one opens with an introduction and a list of shortened terms. A main section then treats lunar return entry in detail. Such documents served flight planning, crew training, and the making of onboard data files for the mission.
nasa-tm-19710020593-cosmic-gamma-radiati:
Cosmic Gamma Radiation from Pion Decay, a NASA preprint numbered X-641-71-254, comments on a paper by Cavallo and Gould. The scan renders its author names illegibly. The subject is the gamma rays produced when cosmic rays strike interstellar gas and create short-lived particles called neutral pions, which then decay.

Earlier calculations of that gamma-ray output, built on accelerator measurements, had largely agreed with each other. Cavallo and Gould's newer results broke that agreement, which prompted this reexamination. The comment concludes that Cavallo and Gould overestimated the gamma-ray production rate from this process. Getting the rate right matters because the glow is a basic tool for studying cosmic rays across the galaxy.
nasa-tm-19710022889-ion-quadrupole-effec:
John V Dugan Jr and Raymond W Palmer of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a July 1971 physics conference in Amsterdam. It studies how a molecule's quadrupole field steers an incoming ion. That steering can decide whether the ion is captured into a brief complex. Such collisions drive much of the chemistry in gases and plasmas.

The authors computed capture chances with numerical methods. They also plotted ion paths on a computer to watch the steering directly. For cold, slowly rotating molecules, capture chances came out near the classic Langevin values. Many captures involved repeated reflections of the ion. Those repeated passes correspond to short lived ion molecule complexes forming.
penelope-s-experiences-in-scotland-being: The sample provided here shows only the front matter of Penelope's Experiences in Scotland, the title page, contents, and the opening verse of chapter one, with no narrative text visible. The title presents the book as extracts from the commonplace book of Penelope Hamilton, by Kate Douglas Wiggin, in a 1913 Gay and Hancock edition. The contents move from Edinburgh society and Holyrood to a wee house in Fife, ballad revels at Rowardennan, and a marriage.
podcast-joerogan-5VoVIpIzj_c:
Investigative writer Annie Jacobsen joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1299. Jacobsen reports on secret government programs, from Area 51 to Pentagon science projects, using declassified files and interviews. Her books read like thrillers, but they rest on documents.

She walks Rogan through the hidden corners of the national security state, including strange weapons research and Cold War schemes. Rogan asks how she verifies stories that officials would rather keep buried. The episode gives listeners a guided tour of real secret history, told by a reporter who insists on sources for every wild claim she prints.
podcast-tuckercarlson-KN36yhie2_c:
Tucker Carlson devotes this episode to the origins of Christian Zionism, the doctrine that Christians must support the modern state of Israel as a biblical duty. His argument is historical and accusatory: the doctrine, he says, was manufactured, corrupted American Christianity from within, and is finally collapsing under its own contradictions.

Carlson traces the teaching through the preachers and publishing empires that spread it, and asks whose interests it served. The episode continues his public break with a pillar of the old Republican coalition. Supporters of the doctrine would call his history a caricature; his audience hears a liberation. Preserved here is the fullest statement of his case, which matters because the argument, once confined to seminaries, now plays out before millions of voters.
the-adventures-of-a-forty-niner-an-histo:
Daniel Knower wrote The Adventures of a Forty-Niner in 1894, an account of California and of San Francisco and its people in the gold rush days. He gave the book to Colonel Jonathan Stevenson, Colonel John C. Fremont, and Captain John A. Sutter, named as the three chief pioneers of California.

Front pages tell of the Society of California Pioneers, formed to keep the memory of those days and guard its members. Only men who reached California before January 1, 1850 could join, with their grown sons let in at age twenty-one. At a San Francisco fair parade the old-timers drew wild cheers. Readers get a pioneer's own mix of tale, civic pride, and street scenes from the rush.
the-exploring-expedition-to-the-rocky-mo:
Brevet Col. J. C. Fremont wrote the report of his government exploring trip to the Rocky Mountains, Oregon, and California, printed here in an 1852 edition. A section on the physical lay of California is added, along with fresh notices of the gold region drawn from recent sources.

The preface praises the trip as a faithful account of land then little known to most readers. It points to the area's climate, people, products, and fitness for farms and towns. Readers get an early survey of the West made just as gold and settlement were drawing crowds there.
the-girl-scout-pioneers-or-winning-the-f: Lillian C. Garis wrote The Girl Scout Pioneers, or Winning the First B. C. The title page also names her Girl Scout books at Bellair and Sea Crest. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list. The heads run from Girls and Girls and Woodland Thrills. They run through A Noble Deed Undone, A Novel Jail, and Tenderfoot Adventures. They also name Clue to the Missing and The Tangled Web, a girls' outdoor tale with a mystery thread.
the-history-of-education-educational-pra:
Ellwood P. Cubberley wrote The History of Education, on educational practice and progress considered as a phase of the development and spread of Western civilization. A preface explains that the volume, with a companion volume of Readings, grew out of a practical teaching need at Stanford University.

Twenty-two years earlier, Cubberley says, he entered Stanford as a professor of education and had to build a syllabus of lectures from the first. He wanted the subject taught as part of the rise and progress of Western civilization. That syllabus grew, was published in book form in 1902, and reached a second, enlarged edition in 1905.
the-lion-of-saint-mark-a-story-of-venice:
G. A. Henty lays his Venice tale in the fourteenth century and opens with a full preface on the city rise. Venice grew, he says, from fugitive settlements on sandy islands in a shallow lagoon. She became a sea power, ruled Adriatic lands, checked the Turks, and took Constantinople.

Henty picks her hardest struggle instead of her triumphs, when Hungary, Padua, and Genoa joined against her. Contents here list twenty chapters, ending with the siege of Chioggia and the triumph of Venice. A boy hero moves through conspiracy, piracy, and sea battles in that fight for survival.
the-olden-time-series-vol-6-literary-cur: Literary Curiosities is volume 6 of the Olden Time Series by Henry M. Brooks of Salem, gleanings from old newspapers, chiefly of Boston and Salem, with his brief comments. Ticknor and Company of Boston began the series in the spring of 1886. Only the publisher's pages and the series list are present here, so the pieces themselves do not appear. The list names all six volumes, from the old lottery and the spinning wheel to strange punishments and this one.
the-organization-of-the-congregation-in-:
Beale M. Schmucker wrote on the organization of the congregation in the early Lutheran churches in America. His paper came from the Lutheran Church Review of July 1887 and was printed in Philadelphia that year. Schmucker argues that the Lutheran church in America had a rare chance to shape its own government, free of the state control known in the old world.

He doubts that any German Lutheran congregation in Pennsylvania had a written constitution before Henry Melchior Muehlenberg arrived. The first known one, at Philadelphia in 1746, was brief and rudimentary. The earliest German congregation, at New Hanover in 1703 under Justus Falckner, left no record of its form. Schmucker follows the slow settling of congregational order.
the-pilgrim-s-progress-from-this-world-t:
John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress, Part One, carries its full title From This World To That Which Is To Come. Editorial notes explain that Part One stands complete in itself. Bunyan wrote a sequel some years later. The part is presented as a dream, and Bible references are marked in the margins for the reader.

Bunyan opens with a verse apology for his book. He says he began writing about the way and race of the saints in the gospel day. An allegory of their journey toward glory came on him unbidden. Twenty points became twenty more, multiplying like sparks from coals of fire. Fearing the new matter would eat out the book already in hand, he set it by itself. The apology, half shy and half bold, introduces a much-read allegory.
the-sea-witch-or-the-african-quadroon-a-:
Lieutenant Murray's The Sea-Witch, or The African Quadroon, bills itself as a story of the slave coast. Its contents run from Outward Bound through a gale, a wreck, and a duel to a denouement. Four shorter pieces by other hands are also listed. A preface by the author follows the contents. A sibling record of the same book carries the same title page and contents.

In that preface, Murray asks readers to take the story in the spirit in which it was written. It is neither a pro-slavery nor an anti-slavery tale, he insists. The peculiar institution enters only as an auxiliary, he says. The plot and the slave-coast locality made some reference necessary. He claims the subject is treated with entire impartiality throughout. His paper, he adds, shall neither directly nor indirectly take a side.
the-shadow-of-the-north-a-story-of-old-n: Joseph A. Altsheler published The Shadow of the North in 1917. Its subtitle is A Story of Old New York and a Lost Campaign. The pages shown give the title and a roster of characters in the French and Indian War series. No chapter text follows. Robert Lennox is a lad of unknown origin, the roster says. Tayoga is a young Onondaga warrior, and David Willet a hunter. Montcalm, Wolfe, and Braddock also appear, along with Joseph Brant in his youth.
the-theory-of-the-theatre-and-other-prin: Clayton Hamilton's Theory of the Theatre and Other Principles of Dramatic Criticism was published by Henry Holt in April 1910 and dedicated to Brander Matthews, his mentor and friend. This record shows the publisher's pages, including a full contents summary of Hamilton's companion volume, Studies in Stagecraft, the title page, and the dedication. Hamilton's own essays on playmaking, stage direction, and dramatic criticism do not begin in the pages present. The advertisement at least maps his wide range, from the pictorial stage to the one-act play in America.
the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-egypt-: Gilbert Parker's Weavers, a tale of England and Egypt of fifty years ago, appears in this complete-edition record with a contents list running through sixty-three chapters. Separate volume records in the library carry the same novel in parts, citing books three through six. This record's own list stops at book four, while the final heading is chapter sixty-three, Honour of Kings. Early chapters take Egypt, a house in Soho Square, and Nahoum the Copt. Later headings promise the thirst of the desert.
the-world-of-romance-being-contributions:
William Morris's early tales, first printed in the Oxford and Cambridge Magazine in 1856, were reissued in 1906 by J. Thomson. A long quotation from J. W. Mackail frames the collection. Mackail describes a world of pure romance in the tales. Medieval customs, buildings, and Catholic religion fill that world. He admits the tales cannot be placed in any known age or country.

Morris later dismissed these youthful stories as crude. Mackail disagrees about their worth. He compares their imagination to Keats's Endymion. Their language, he says, runs rich and irregularly gorgeous. Readers meet Morris before his fame in design and socialism. Medieval dreaming already shapes his distinctive voice.
theatrum-chemicum-zetzner-1602-c:
Yet another volume of the 1602 Strasbourg Theatrum Chemicum carries Zetzner's project further still. Lazarus Zetzner printed tract after tract by the most trusted alchemical authorities. The aim was a complete library of the art between a few covers.

The texts treat metals, spirits, salts, and the famed stone of the wise. They speak in riddles, images, and workshop rules all at once. For adepts, owning the full set meant owning the past of their craft. Volume by volume, readers can watch the seventeenth-century canon of alchemy take shape in print, just as its first owners saw it.
un-ga-res-51-198-c:
Peace in Guatemala was taking hold when the General Assembly passed Resolution 51/198 C in 1997. The UN Verification Mission in Guatemala had just had its mandate stretched to 31 March 1998. A deal on a firm cease-fire was being put into force on time. The Assembly had the Secretary-General's report on the checking of the peace deals before it.

The report is welcomed, and praise goes wide. The state of Guatemala, the rebel front known as the URNG, and the people, bodies, and groups of the land are all praised for their part in the work. All are urged to join forces for the next phase of the peace plan, which ran to the end of 1997.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 51/198 C, adopted on 31 July 1997, followed up on the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala. The Assembly had extended its mandate to 31 March 1998. The hosted text, which is partly cut short, welcomes the Secretary-General's report on the mission. It notes the on-time carrying-out of the Agreement on the Definitive Ceasefire. It restates full support for the peace accords' broad agenda of democratic, fair, and multicultural growth. It invites the world community to keep helping make its aims real.
why-and-how-a-hand-book-for-the-use-of-t: Only the title page and contents are present here for Why and How, a handbook for temperance unions in Canada, so the guidance itself does not appear. Mrs. Addie Chisholm, president of the Ontario union, wrote the book for the W. C. T. U. The contents open with chapters named Suffering and Awakening. Work and organization come next. Later chapters ask why women should work and how they may work. A chapter tells how to form a local union. Questions and answers close the list.
